somalia.content: Feisal Mohamed Hashi: The Vision Behind Somalia's Revenue Reforms - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Feisal Mohamed Hashi: The Vision Behind Somalia's Revenue Reforms Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Adan Omar Hashi Friday November 13, 2026 Somalia has reached a turning point. After years of relying on external support, it is learning to stand on its own. Debt relief has been secured, investor interest is growing, and the first petroleum licences are on the horizon. Much of that progress rests on governance reform and stronger domestic revenue mobilisation, which have steadied the public finances and supported renewed economic growth. Whether any of this ends up paying for schools, roads and clinics will depend on something far less visible: the everyday work of collecting revenue, and the people who do it. In the end, the leaders who matter most are the ones who build institutions that outlast them. On 12 November 2026, the Council of Ministers of the Federal Government of Somalia appointed Feisal Mohamed Hashi as Director General of the newly formed Somali Revenue Authority (SRA). For anyone who has followed Somalia's fiscal reforms, the choice came as no surprise. Hashi had spent the previous three and a half years as Director General of Revenue at the Ministry of Finance, where he led the modernisation of tax administration, the strengthening of customs and the drive for domestic revenue mobilisation that made an independent authority possible in the first place. The man behind the reforms advertisements Hashi has become the Authority's first leader, having helped drive the changes that gave rise to it. An expert in domestic revenue and political economy with more than twelve years' experience, he brings deep technical and institutional knowledge to the job. The reform agenda he now leads is, in large part, one he designed. Hashi built his career inside Somalia's own institutions. Over twelve years in public financial management, economic policy and revenue mobilisation, he rose through the Ministry of Finance, serving as Head of Budget Execution and Head of the Macroeconomic Policy and Analysis Unit, before taking charge of the Revenue Directorate in May 2023. Those posts gave him budget discipline, macroeconomic analysis, revenue forecasting and, eventually, hands-on command of the country's tax and customs operations. Few officials reach the top of a revenue administration having seen it from so many sides, let alone having helped rebuild it. His academic background points the same way. He holds a Bachelor's degree in Accounting from SIMAD University and a Master's in Economic Development from Ritsumeikan University in Japan, with further international training in public financial management, economic planning and revenue forecasting. He also taught Economic Planning and Financial Management at Somali National University between 2020 and 2023, part of a long-standing interest in developing other people's skills. His expertise spans tax reform, customs administration, fiscal federalism, revenue forecasting and the design of legal and regulatory frameworks. That last area, the patient drafting of laws and shaping of institutions, best captures how he works, and it led directly to the groundwork for setting up the Authority he now leads. The timing is deliberate. It comes as the Federal Government places domestic revenue at the centre of its economic strategy, pushing to raise collections and modernise the tax system after years of leaning heavily on external support. Appointing the official who led that drive at the Ministry to run the new Authority is a clear signal that the same momentum is meant to carry into it. A directorate transformed When Hashi took over the Revenue Directorate in 2023, it handled both inland revenue and customs with limited systems and a heavy reliance on manual processes. Under him, the Directorate pushed reform across the board: tightening compliance, widening the tax base, improving taxpayer services, strengthening customs and bringing in digital tools across the collection chain. It also took on a bigger policy role, advising the government on how to raise domestic revenue without choking the private sector it relies on. One idea ran through all these reforms: Somalia should pay for its own future from its own resources, and the body that collects them should be transparent, efficient and professional enough to earn public trust. ITAS: more than software One of the clearest examples of that idea, and the reform most closely associated with Hashi, is the Integrated Tax Administration System (ITAS), which he drove forward at the Directorate. ITAS looks like an IT project, but it is really a change in how the Somali state deals with its taxpayers. By bringing registration, filing, payment, compliance monitoring, reporting and data management onto a single digital platform, it is designed to replace paper trails and personal discretion with records, rules and audit logs. For taxpayers, it will mean simpler compliance, less paperwork and a system that treats them as customers, not suspects. For government, it will mean stronger oversight, cleaner data, better forecasting, sharper audits and fewer chances for revenue to leak between assessment and the Treasury. A single record of every taxpayer will also make risk-based auditing and modern compliance management possible. The rollout of ITAS, due to begin at the end of 2026 and run into 2027, is likely to be remembered as one of the turning points in Somalia's public financial management reforms: the moment modernisation becomes visible to ordinary taxpayers, through the platform the Somali Revenue Authority will carry forward. The same shift can already be seen in other parts of the government. At the port, the Somalia Customs Automated System (SOMCAS) has moved customs processing onto a digital platform, while immigration has brought visa-fee collection online. In each case, the move away from manual, cash-based handling, which bred corruption and lost revenue, to digital systems has made collection more transparent and far harder to divert. Financing the state from within Hashi's core argument is simple: a state that cannot raise its own finance cannot set its own priorities. He has pressed for domestic revenue mobilisation as a national cause, not just a technical target. The payoff is not really in any one year's collection figure. It is in the structure now behind it: a revenue system built around compliance, efficiency and digitalisation, designed to keep working no matter who is in charge, and now carried into the Somali Revenue Authority. The reforms were meant to raise performance and support the wider economic agenda, but their real aim was to create systems that can keep collections growing for years and convince the public that taxes are assessed fairly and spent well. The Somali Revenue Authority is where that work now lives, and where its future will be decided. Laying the legal groundwork One of the most lasting parts of Hashi's record is also one of the least visible: his work on the legal framework that now governs Somalia's revenue and fiscal institutions. He gave technical input to a series of laws that will shape the country's finances for a generation: The Revenue Administration Law (RAL), which gives domestic revenue administration a dedicated legal foundation, defines powers and responsibilities, and anchors accountability in statute rather than practice. The Income Tax Law (ITL), which modernises the basis for income taxation and gives taxpayers and investors a more predictable and transparent environment. The Extractive Industries Fiscal Regime Law (EIFRL), which sets out how Somalia will tax its emerging petroleum and mineral sectors so that resource wealth is converted into lasting benefits for citizens. The Petroleum Fiscal Regime Regulation (PFRR), which supplies the detailed rules needed to administer petroleum taxation and readies institutions for future resource revenues. Together, these laws and regulations clarify who does what, strengthen tax and customs administration, and give the new Authority solid legal footing to build on. From directorate to authority Setting up the Somali Revenue Authority as an independent institution is one of the more significant fiscal developments in Somalia's recent history. Giving revenue administration its own autonomous base is meant to build professional capacity, embed transparency and accountability, raise domestic revenue and give the state a firmer foundation for growth. The Authority is expected to become the central body for administering domestic taxes and customs revenues, with a coordinated, digitalisation-driven approach. Over time, it will largely determine how public services are financed and how fast Somalia can reduce its reliance on foreign aid. Hashi's appointment as Director General puts him at the centre of this transition. The reforms he led at the Directorate, among them ITAS, the legislative programme and the compliance drive, now move into the new institution under the same leadership. Across Africa and beyond, revenue authorities have become mainstays of national development and economic governance, raising collections, professionalising staff and shielding revenue from day-to-day politics. Somalia's SRA could do the same. Preparing for oil before the first barrel Perhaps the most forward-looking part of Hashi's agenda concerns a sector that earns Somalia nothing yet: extractives. Somalia is close to developing petroleum and minerals, and the record of other resource-rich countries is sobering. Countries that build their fiscal institutions only after production starts tend to lose revenue, mishandle investors and forfeit public trust. Those that prepare early capture more value and protect the national interest better. In recognition of this, the revenue reform agenda included the creation of a specialised Extractive Taxation Unit, a deliberate investment in expertise, administrative capacity and fiscal governance years ahead of commercial production. The Unit's purpose is to master the complex regimes that govern petroleum and mining taxation, from cost recovery and ring-fencing to transfer pricing and production sharing, so that when revenues arrive, the state is ready to assess, audit and collect them. It also gives Somalia a credible counterpart for international operators, whose own tax teams are large, experienced and well advised. It is unglamorous work. But how well a country governs its resources is largely settled before the first barrel is pumped or the first shipment leaves port, and Somalia has chosen to settle it early. Institutions that outlast their founders A public servant is best judged not by the revenue collected in a single year but by the institutions left behind. On that measure, Hashi stands out, which helps explain the broad support for his appointment. He has consistently chosen structural change over quick wins: better systems, stronger organisations, effective laws and regulation, a sustained digitalisation drive, taxpayer education and early preparation for what lies ahead. Taken together, the past three years of reform amount to a single plan, not just a list of projects. The road ahead Somalia's economic future depends on whether its institutions can turn today's openings into lasting prosperity, and revenue administration is central to that. The next few years will be shaped by the full rollout of ITAS, further tax administration reform, the SRA becoming operational, continued gains in domestic revenue and the arrival of extractive revenues that will need careful management. Delivering all of it now rests with the Somali Revenue Authority, and with the official who did most to build it. Visionary leaders are usually remembered for the systems they changed, not the offices they held. If Somalia manages to build a modern, accountable revenue authority that can fund the country's development and handle its resource wealth responsibly, Feisal Mohamed Hashi's mark will be on it: the digital platform taxpayers will use, the laws that bind the state, the Authority he now leads, and the expertise waiting for the first barrel. (Reuters Photo) Mogadishu (HOL) — Türkiye's Ministry of National Defence has denied reports that it plans to deploy 15,000 troops to Somalia at the request of the federal government, reaffirming its commitment to military training and counterterrorism cooperation with Mogadishu. Speaking at a news briefing Thursday, ministry spokesperson Rear Adm. Zeki Aktürk rejected claims circulating in Turkish and Somali media about a large-scale deployment of Turkish forces to Somalia. “Claims that Türkiye will send 15,000 troops to Somalia at the request of the Somali government do not reflect the truth,” the ministry said. advertisements Aktürk confirmed that Türkiye already maintains a military presence in Somalia through the Somali-Turkish Task Force and an air component command. He said Turkish forces would continue supporting Somalia's counterterrorism capabilities through military assistance, training and advisory services. The denial follows reports suggesting that Somalia had sought additional military assistance from international partners, including Türkiye, amid concerns about security as African Union troop-contributing countries prepare to withdraw some of their forces. Some reports also alleged that fighters from Syrian armed groups involved in the overthrow of the former Syrian government could be deployed to Somalia. Those claims have not been substantiated. Türkiye operates the TURKSOM military training facility in Mogadishu, where Turkish instructors have trained Somali military personnel as part of efforts to strengthen the Somali National Army. adinsideThe facility, which opened in 2017, has played a significant role in developing Somalia's military capabilities, including training specialized units involved in operations against al-Shabab. The Turkish statement comes days after Turkish Ambassador to Somalia Ferhat Alkan met Somali National Security Adviser Aweys Haji Yusuf Ahmed in Mogadishu to discuss military cooperation, counterterrorism operations and regional security developments. During Tuesday's meeting, the two officials reviewed Somalia's security situation and efforts to strengthen cooperation between the countries as African Union forces prepare for changes to their deployments. “Türkiye continues to contribute to the peace, stability and security of Somalia, as it has in the past,” the Turkish Embassy said following the meeting. According to Somalia's Office of the National Security Adviser, the discussions also covered political developments, operations against al-Shabab and broader bilateral cooperation. The office said Somalia appreciated Türkiye's longstanding support and emphasized the importance of continued coordination to strengthen national security. The discussions come amid uncertainty over the future of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), particularly following Uganda's announcement that it would withdraw troops deployed under bilateral arrangements and gradually end its participation in the mission. Uganda has been one of the largest contributors to African Union military operations in Somalia since 2007, playing a major role in securing Mogadishu and supporting operations against al-Shabab. The withdrawal plans have raised concerns about the readiness of Somali forces to assume responsibility for areas previously secured by foreign troops. Somalia and Türkiye maintain a longstanding defense partnership covering military training, counterterrorism, maritime security and military capacity-building. Despite rejecting reports of an additional 15,000 troops, Ankara reaffirmed that its existing military mission would continue supporting Somalia's efforts to strengthen its armed forces and combat militant groups. According to a statement from the Turkish embassy, the meeting with Sheikh Sharif focused on the latest developments in Somalia, the political process, and the importance of continued dialogue and consultation. The two also recalled the historic visit of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and First Lady Emine Erdoğan to Mogadishu in 2011, when Sheikh Sharif was president and welcomed the Turkish leader. Ambassador Alkan thanked Sheikh Sharif for his hospitality and the exchange of views. The meeting with Sheikh Sharif follows Alkan’s separate talks with Farmaajo on Monday, which the embassy described as part of his introductory engagements, covering Somalia’s political developments and bilateral relations, as reported in the coverage of the Farmaajo meeting . He also met Khaire, with discussions focused on the political process and the efforts of the Quartet, the group of Türkiye, the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union that is facilitating the upcoming dialogue, as detailed in the coverage of Türkiye’s mediation efforts . A Mediator Engaging the Opposition Alkan’s meetings with opposition figures are significant because they come as Türkiye positions itself as a facilitator in Somalia’s political crisis. Türkiye’s intelligence service has been involved in mediating the dispute over the legitimacy of the government since June, when a delegation led by the deputy director of the National Intelligence Organization arrived to encourage negotiations, as reported by the Middle East Forum. But Türkiye’s role is not without controversy. The same report noted that many opposition parties distrust Türkiye as a mediator because Ankara is simultaneously arming and training the federal forces whose commander-in-chief is the subject of the dispute. Puntland and Jubaland declined to participate in the Turkish-facilitated format, and the opposition has asked for broader international mediation. The Quartet framework, which includes the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union alongside Türkiye, is an attempt to address that concern. The four partners have agreed to facilitate the November 14-18 dialogue, with an agenda that includes meetings among political leaders, a declaration of the basic principles of an agreement, and consultations by technical committees, as reported in the coverage of the Quartet’s role . Sheikh Sharif’s participation in the political process is particularly important. He is a member of the Somali Future Council, which has been weighing whether to attend the November forum. The council held a tense meeting at his residence in late October to debate the invitation, with some members inclined to accept and others pushing for conditions, as reported in the coverage of the Future Council’s deliberations . Alkan’s meeting with Sheikh Sharif is a signal that Türkiye is engaging directly with the figures whose decisions will determine whether the forum proceeds with broad participation. Critical Note Ambassador Alkan’s meetings with Farmaajo, Khaire, and Sheikh Sharif are a diplomatic outreach campaign, and they should be reported as such. Türkiye is not a neutral party in Somalia’s political crisis. It has trained and equipped the forces at the center of the dispute, and its intelligence service has been involved in the mediation efforts. But it is also one of the few external actors with the access and influence to bring the government and opposition to the same table. The opposition’s distrust of Türkiye is understandable. A mediator who is also a military partner of one of the parties is not an ideal broker. The Quartet framework is designed to address that problem by broadening the mediation beyond Ankara. Whether it succeeds will depend on whether the opposition believes the Quartet can deliver a process that is not simply a ratification of the government’s terms. Alkan’s meetings are a sign that Türkiye is listening to the opposition, not just the government. That is a necessary step. It is not a guarantee. The November forum is scheduled to begin on Saturday, and it remains unclear whether the Future Council, the Salvation Forum, and Nabad iyo Nolol will attend. The ambassador has opened channels. The question is whether those channels will be used to negotiate or to manage a divided opposition. As Ankara expands its military and economic footprint in Somalia and Beijing pursues its strategic interests in the Horn of Africa, Somaliland is increasingly looking towards India as a natural partner. New Delhi must recognise that the geopolitical contest unfolding along the Gulf of Aden is not merely about African politics. It is about the future balance of power in the Indian Ocean. The Horn of Africa is emerging as one of the most consequential geopolitical theatres of the twenty-first century. What was once viewed primarily through the lens of piracy, terrorism, humanitarian crises and political instability has become an arena where regional and global powers are competing for influence over strategic maritime routes, military access, natural resources and political relationships. Two countries whose expanding presence deserves India’s particular attention are Turkey and China. Both have invested considerable diplomatic and strategic capital in Somalia. Both support Mogadishu’s territorial integrity and oppose Somaliland’s claim to independent sovereignty. Yet their interests extend beyond the question of Somali unity. Turkey sees Somalia as a gateway to expanding its influence across Africa and the Indian Ocean. China views the region through the wider prism of maritime security, economic connectivity, diplomatic influence and its competition with Taiwan. Caught between these ambitions is Somaliland, a territory that restored its claim to independence in 1991 and has since developed its own governing institutions, security structures and political identity. What makes this geopolitical equation particularly interesting is Somaliland’s growing interest in India. While Turkey and China are consolidating their relationships with Mogadishu, Somaliland is signalling that it sees New Delhi as a potentially important partner in its political and economic future. India would be making a strategic mistake if it failed to understand the significance of that opportunity. Turkey ’ s Growing Military Ambitions in Somalia Turkey’s involvement in Somalia did not begin with military ambitions. Ankara initially established its influence through humanitarian assistance, infrastructure development and diplomatic engagement, particularly following the devastating famine of 2011. Over time, however, that humanitarian relationship evolved into a comprehensive strategic partnership. Today, Turkey operates the TURKSOM military training facility in Mogadishu, which opened in 2017 and has trained thousands of Somali military personnel. Turkish assistance includes military training, counterterrorism cooperation, defence equipment and institutional capacity-building. The relationship has become increasingly significant. On November 11, 2026, reports confirmed fresh discussions between Turkish and Somali officials on expanding military and security cooperation. But military training is only one dimension of Ankara’s ambitions. Turkey has also secured agreements covering offshore petroleum exploration, maritime security and fisheries governance. Its state-owned petroleum company has exploration rights in three offshore blocks, while a Turkish military-linked investment institution has acquired a significant role in Somalia’s fisheries administration. This brings us to a development that should concern Indian strategic planners. Turkey is developing a space launch facility on Somalia’s Indian Ocean coastline. Although presented as a civilian space programme, reports based on Turkish government documents and parliamentary testimony indicate potential applications for long-range missile testing. A November 9, 2026 investigation reported that the Turkish Space Agency had allocated approximately 2.1 billion Turkish lira, equivalent to $42 million, for transfer to Turkey’s Defence Industry Support Fund under its national space-access programme. The reported financial connection raises legitimate questions about the project’s dual-use potential, although it does not establish that the entire allocation is being spent on missile infrastructure. India must assess these developments carefully. A Turkish military and technological presence on the African coast of the Indian Ocean does not automatically constitute a threat to India. Turkey is not China’s military ally, and the two countries pursue distinct geopolitical agendas. Nevertheless, any expansion of foreign military capabilities near important Indian Ocean shipping routes warrants serious strategic attention. The question is no longer simply what Turkey is doing in Somalia. The question is what Turkey’s growing military, maritime and economic influence could mean for the future balance of power across the western Indian Ocean. China ’ s Somalia Strategy: Somaliland and the Taiwan Question China’s approach to Somalia is different from Turkey’s, but no less consequential. Beijing’s primary interests include protecting its diplomatic influence, expanding commercial relationships, securing maritime access and limiting Taiwan’s international partnerships. Somalia has consistently supported Beijing’s One China position. In return, China has strongly defended Somalia’s territorial integrity, including its claim over Somaliland. For China, Somaliland presents a particular diplomatic challenge. In 2020, Somaliland and Taiwan established representative offices in each other’s capitals. Their relationship has subsequently expanded into development, technical and diplomatic cooperation. In June 2026, Somaliland opened a new representative office in Taiwan, reaffirming its determination to pursue independent international relationships despite objections from Beijing and Mogadishu. This relationship carries implications beyond symbolic diplomacy. Somaliland has demonstrated that it is willing to maintain a partnership with Taiwan even when doing so complicates its relations with one of the world’s most powerful countries. China has responded by strengthening its opposition to Somaliland’s recognition. On October 23, 2026, China and Djibouti issued a joint statement reaffirming Somalia’s territorial integrity, rejecting Somaliland’s recognition and opposing Somaliland’s cooperation with Taiwan. aa.com.tr The significance of this development should not be underestimated. China already maintains a military support base in neighbouring Djibouti. Its economic and security interests extend across the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. Somaliland’s coastline, particularly the port of Berbera and its proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb maritime corridor, occupies an important position in this strategic geography. For Beijing, the Somaliland question therefore intersects with three considerations: Somalia’s territorial claims, China’s competition with Taiwan, and its broader regional influence. For Somaliland, the challenge is equally clear. How does a relatively small territory defend its political autonomy and economic interests while facing opposition from a major global power? One possible answer lies in diversifying its international relationships. And that is where India enters the equation. Somaliland: A Nation Seeking Partners, Not Patrons I recently had the opportunity to visit Somaliland and engage with its leadership, including President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, popularly known as Irro. My discussions reinforced an important impression: Somaliland’s leadership is not merely seeking diplomatic recognition. It is looking for meaningful economic partnerships, international investment, technological cooperation and opportunities for its young population. There is a strong desire to transform Somaliland from a territory struggling for international acceptance into an economically productive and strategically relevant nation. Its leadership understands the importance of geography. Somaliland occupies a valuable position along the Gulf of Aden, with access to maritime routes connecting the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. Its opportunities extend across ports, logistics, energy exploration, fisheries, renewable energy, healthcare, education, digital infrastructure and industrial development. But geography alone cannot transform an economy. Somaliland needs capital, technology, institutional expertise and international partnerships. What I found particularly encouraging was the interest in developing closer relationships with India. India is viewed as a country with considerable expertise in healthcare, pharmaceuticals, education, information technology, infrastructure, entrepreneurship and affordable technological solutions. There is also an appreciation for India’s historical connections with the wider Horn of Africa. In my assessment, Somaliland sees India not simply as another foreign power but as a potential partner in its long-term development. This distinction matters. Somaliland does not need to become a battleground between China, Turkey and India. It needs the freedom to develop relationships that serve the aspirations of its people. India can contribute to that aspiration without reproducing the geopolitical rivalries that have complicated the development of other regions. Why Somaliland Matters to India ’ s Indian Ocean Strategy India’s strategic community has traditionally concentrated much of its attention on the eastern Indian Ocean, the Strait of Malacca and China’s activities in South Asia. However, the western Indian Ocean is becoming equally important. The Gulf of Aden connects Indian maritime commerce to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. Disruptions along these routes can affect India’s trade, energy security and commercial interests. Somaliland’s location makes it relevant to this maritime equation. The ports of Berbera, Zeila, Bulhar and Lughaya offer different possibilities for future commercial and infrastructure development, although their operational readiness and investment requirements vary substantially. For India, the opportunities could include commercial port participation, maritime logistics, energy exploration, telecommunications, healthcare, educational partnerships and industrial infrastructure. There is also a longer-term strategic consideration. India’s SAGAR vision and its wider approach to maritime security emphasise cooperative security, regional development and respect for the interests of partner countries. Somaliland could eventually become a meaningful participant in this framework, subject to diplomatic and legal considerations. India should also recognise that commercial engagement and diplomatic recognition are separate questions. New Delhi has maintained longstanding relations with Somalia and publicly reaffirmed its respect for Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity in January 2026. That position creates diplomatic complexities which cannot simply be ignored. However, it should not prevent India from studying Somaliland’s economic potential, expanding people-to-people relationships or examining legally viable forms of cooperation. India’s strategic interests require both diplomatic prudence and geopolitical foresight. Turkey and China Have Different Objectives, but Somaliland Faces a Common Challenge It would be inaccurate to suggest that Turkey and China are operating a coordinated strategy against Somaliland. They are not. Turkey’s relationship with Somalia is driven substantially by defence cooperation, economic opportunities, maritime influence and its ambition to establish itself as an important power in Africa. China’s position is shaped by its support for Somalia’s territorial integrity, its opposition to Taiwan’s diplomatic engagement and its wider economic and security interests. Yet both countries’ positions have consequences for Somaliland. Both oppose its independent sovereignty, and both maintain relationships with Mogadishu that strengthen Somalia’s international standing. The practical result is that Somaliland faces significant external diplomatic pressure while attempting to build its own economic future. There is another important dimension. Somaliland’s relative institutional continuity since 1991 deserves greater international attention. Its experience has not been without political tensions, territorial disputes or governance challenges. Nevertheless, it has developed functioning institutions and demonstrated an ability to sustain a substantial degree of self-government. That experience merits serious examination rather than automatic dismissal. The international community cannot indefinitely discuss Somaliland solely through the political preferences of Mogadishu without examining the historical, legal and democratic arguments advanced by Somalilanders themselves. The African Union, in particular, should engage these arguments with greater intellectual and institutional openness. India Must Not Allow Strategic Opportunities to Pass Unnoticed India does not need to confront Turkey or China over Somaliland. Nor should New Delhi approach Somaliland as a geopolitical instrument to be deployed against Beijing or Ankara. Such an approach would undermine the very partnership India should seek to build. Instead, India should adopt a constructive, phased strategy. The immediate priority should be commercial and developmental engagement. Indian companies possess considerable capabilities in port management, energy services, telecommunications, pharmaceuticals, healthcare, agriculture, renewable energy, technology and vocational education. These are precisely the sectors that could help Somaliland generate employment, develop its infrastructure and strengthen its economy. Healthcare deserves particular attention. Somaliland patients seeking specialised treatment abroad face logistical and financial challenges. India, with its established medical institutions and comparatively affordable healthcare, could become an important destination for Somaliland patients. A more efficient medical travel framework, alongside hospital partnerships and training programmes, would provide tangible humanitarian benefits. Similarly, Indian universities and technical institutions could help develop Somaliland’s future workforce. Technology partnerships could support digital governance, public services, entrepreneurship and industrial development. Commercial port investments could strengthen regional trade connectivity, provided projects are commercially viable and legally structured. These initiatives would build relationships through practical outcomes rather than geopolitical rhetoric. Over time, India could consider more formal mechanisms of engagement consistent with its broader diplomatic interests. The question of recognition deserves a serious and independent Indian assessment, informed by international law, Somaliland’s history, regional stability and India’s long-term strategic interests. I personally believe India should recognise Somaliland’s sovereignty. But I also recognise that such a decision requires careful diplomatic preparation. Recognition should be the outcome of a considered national strategy, not an impulsive reaction to the activities of other countries. The Larger Contest Is About Influence Over the Future There is a tendency to view the Horn of Africa as a peripheral region. That perception is outdated. The region sits at the intersection of African economic development, Middle Eastern security, Indian Ocean trade and the strategic ambitions of major powers. Turkey understands this. China understands this. The Gulf states understand this. India must understand it too. The emergence of Somaliland as a potential economic and strategic partner presents an opportunity for New Delhi to deepen its presence in a region whose importance will only increase. It is also an opportunity to demonstrate a different model of international partnership. India can engage Somaliland through mutual respect, technology transfer, investment, institutional development and people-to-people cooperation. Such engagement need not come at the expense of India’s relations with Somalia. Indeed, a carefully designed Indian approach could contribute to wider regional prosperity and stability. Somaliland Is Extending Its Hand. Will India Respond? The geopolitical reality is becoming increasingly evident. Turkey is strengthening its military and economic influence in Somalia. China is consolidating its diplomatic position while opposing Somaliland’s relationship with Taiwan and its aspirations for international recognition. Somaliland, meanwhile, is looking beyond its immediate neighbourhood for partners willing to understand its aspirations and contribute to its development. India has an opportunity to be one of those partners. My interactions in Somaliland convinced me that there is genuine interest in building a meaningful relationship with India. I believe that interest should be reciprocated through serious diplomatic consideration and practical economic engagement. India does not have to compete with Turkey or China on their terms. It must act according to its own strategic interests and the principles that have guided its international relationships. The future of the Horn of Africa will not be determined by military bases and diplomatic declarations alone. It will also be shaped by which countries help create sustainable economic opportunities, strengthen institutions and improve the lives of ordinary people. Somaliland is extending its hand towards India. The question is whether New Delhi will recognise the strategic value of that gesture before others determine the geopolitical future of the region. somalia.content: Ghana earn first Cup of Nations qualifying points in 2-0 win over Somalia - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SPORTS Ghana earn first Cup of Nations qualifying points in 2-0 win over Somalia Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Mark Gleeson Friday November 13, 2026 Four-times winners Ghana picked up their first Africa Cup of Nations qualifying points on ‌Thursday even if they had to sweat to beat lowly-ranked Somalia 2-0 in Sekondi to join other past champions posting victories. Democratic Republic of Congo beat Sierra Leone 3-1 at home, Cameroon secured a 2-0 home over Namibia and Ivory Cost overcame Gambia 2-1. Senegal, who ​are awaiting a court decision on their status as Africa champions, posted a 4-1 triumph over Sudan ​in new coach Patrick Vieira’s home debut. advertisements Ghana lost their opening two Group C games in ⁠a shock setback at the start of the 2027 qualifying campaign and fired veteran coach Carlos Queiroz, putting ​women’s team coach Kim-Lars Bjorkegren temporarily in charge. Captain Jordan Ayew had his 14th-minute penalty saved as 200th-ranked Somalia proved ​stubborn opposition but Jonas Adjetey’s header in first-half stoppage time put the home side ahead and Felix Afena-Gyna added a second soon after the break. DR Congo, who like Ghana reached the second round at the this year's World Cup, moved closer to securing early ​qualification as they won a third successive Group E game. WISSA GOAL Yoane Wissa’ fourth-minute goal set the platform, and ​Samuel Moutoussamy made it 2-0 in the 35th minute with a superb right-footed strike into the top corner before midfielder Edo Kayembe ‌added ⁠a third early in the second half. The Congolese, with three qualifiers left, are five points clear of Equatorial Guinea and Zimbabwe, who played out a goalless draw on Thursday. Senegal were being held 1-1 at halftime by Sudan after Nicolas Jackson opened the scoring, but Mohamed Abuaagla equalised. Boulaye Dia, Ibrahim Mbaye and debutant Pathe Mboup scored in the ​second half to ensure Senegal ​top Group J. Cameroon fielded ⁠a youthful side with 27-year-old captain Bryan Mbeumo the oldest player but were still too strong for Namibia as Saidou Alioum and Bil Nsongo scored in the first half ​hour in Douala. Ivory Coast struggled at home to tiny Gambia, who had upset ​Ghana 4-2 away ⁠in their last game in September. Malick Yalcouye and Elye Wahi put Ivory Coast ahead in Bouake, but Musa Barrow pulled one back to ensure an uncomfortable finish for the hosts. Benin trounced the Central African Republic 4-1 in Group F with ⁠a double ​from Aiyegun Tosin while Guinea beat Eritrea 2-1 in Group D. There ​are 12 qualifiers scheduled for Friday and threeon Saturday as the group preliminaries reach the halfway mark. The finals are being co-hosted by Kenya, ​Tanzania and Uganda from June 19-July 17 next year. (أرشيفية) الرياض ـ الرياضية 2026.11.11 | 12:22 am انضم فريق الهلال السوداني الأول لكرة القدم إلى قائمة أبطال فازوا بلقب الدوري من داخل غرف المكاتب بعد معارك قانونية ونزاعات قضائية. واسترد الفريق السوداني لقب الدوري الممتاز «النخبة»، الثلاثاء بقرار من لجنة الاستئناف في الاتحاد المحلي بعد سحبه منه سابقًا ومنحه إلى غريمه المريخ. وتعود تفاصيل القضية حينما كسب الأزرق مواجهة الديربي أمام نده الأحمر بهدف نظيف في المباراة النهائية للبطولة التي جرت في العاشر من يونيو الماضي، ليتوج رسميًا باللقب، لكنه تفاجأ لاحقًا بصدور قرار من لجنة الاستئناف يقضي بسحب اللقب منه ومنحه للمريخ الذي عد فائزًا بنتيجة 2-0 على خلفية احتجاجه على عدم قانونية بعض اللاعبين المجنسين في صفوف الفريق الهلالي. وأثار القرار حفيظة إدارة الهلال التي سارعت إلى استئناف مستندة في ذلك على وثائق قانونية، وعلى ضوء ذلك أصدرت لجنة الاستئناف قرارًا يقضي بإلغاء سحب النقاط، واعتماد نتيجة المباراة التي كسبها 1-0، ليستعيد اللقب بعد أكثر من ثلاثة أشهر من تجريده. شهدت الملاعب الكروية العربية والأفريقية أخيرًا وتاريخيًا حالات شهيرة حُسم فيها لقب الدوري داخل غرف مكاتب اللجان القانونية وليس في الملعب فقط. يُعد نادي الهلال السوداني أحدث وأبرز نموذج لحسم لقب الدوري بعد كسب طلب فحص واستئناف لصالحه، إلى جانب حالات أخرى مماثلة مثل نادي الكويت الكويتي. ولم يكن الهلال السوداني هو الوحيد الذي ينجح في كسب استئناف يمنحه لقب بطولة، وسبقه عديد من الأندية ومنهم إنتر ميلان الإيطالي والكويت الكويتي. ففي إيطاليا، أصدرت محكمة الاستئناف التابعة للاتحاد المحلي حكمًا تاريخيًا قضى بسحب لقب موسم 2004- 2005 وإلغائه، في حين قضى القرار القانوني بمنح لقب موسم 2005-2006 لصالح نادي إنتر ميلان الذي كان ثالثًا في الترتيب خلف يوفنتوس وميلان المعاقبين، ليتحول اللقب بقرار المكاتب الإدارية. وجاء ذلك القرار على خلفية قضية التلاعب الشهيرة في إيطاليا والمعروفة بـ «كالتشيو بولي»، وأسفرت عن تجريد بطل وتتويج آخر بقرار اللجان القانونية. أما في الكويت، فقد حسم لقب الدوري موسم 2016-2017 بعد صراع قضائي طويل فيما عرف إعلاميًا آنذاك بـ«أزمة النقاط الثلاث». وتفجرت الأزمة بعدما قدم النادي العربي احتجاجًا على فهد الهاجري لاعب الكويت بحجة الإيقاف، وأيدت لجنة الاستئناف الاحتجاج وأصدرت قرارًا باعتبار العربي فائزًا وسحب النقاط من الكويت، الأمر الذي قرب القادسية من منصة التتويج باللقب. ولم تصمت إدارة الكويت على قرار سحب النقاط الثلاث، واستأنفته أمام محكمة الاستئناف الإدارية التي أصدرت حكمًا نهائيًا ألغى قرار لجنة الانضباط والاستئناف بالاتحاد، وأعاد النقاط الثلاث إلى فريق الكويت ما اسهم بشكل كبير في تتويجه بطلًا للدوري. تصغير تكبير مشاركة مشاركة تابع - 15:30 استعاد نادي الهلال لقب الدوري السوداني الممتاز لكرة القدم لموسم 2025-2026، الثلاثاء، بقرار من لجنة الاستئنافات بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، التي ألغت قرار رابطة الدوري السابق بمنح غريمه التقليدي المريخ نقاط مباراة القمة، واعتمدت نتيجة المواجهة وفق ما ورد في تقرير حكم المباراة. وأعلن الهلال، في بيان رسمي عبر حسابه على “فيسبوك”، أن لجنة الاستئنافات قبلت طلب المراجعة الذي تقدم به النادي شكلًا وموضوعًا، وألغت قرارها السابق القاضي بتحويل نقاط مباراة القمة إلى المريخ الخرطوم. وأوضح النادي أن اللجنة، برئاسة محمد حمد البشير، وعضوية محمد عيسى وزهير عبد الملك والزين الدخيري مقررًا، عقدت اجتماعين يومي 9 و10 نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني الجاري، لمراجعة الطلب والمستندات المرفقة، قبل أن تقرر اعتماد نتيجة المباراة كما وردت في تقرير الحكم. وقال الهلال في بيانه: “بموجب القرار، عاد اللقب إلى خزائن سيد البلد، ليواصل النادي تأكيد مكانته بوصفه النادي الأكثر تتويجًا بالبطولات في السودان”. وتعود تفاصيل القضية إلى مواجهة القمة التي جمعت الهلال والمريخ في يونيو/حزيران الماضي، وانتهت بفوز الهلال بهدف، حيث تقدم المريخ بشكوى رسمية اتهم فيها الهلال بإشراك 8 لاعبين أجانب، رغم أن لوائح المسابقة تسمح بمشاركة 5 لاعبين أجانب فقط. وأصدرت رابطة الدوري السوداني في الشهر التالي قرارًا باعتبار الهلال خاسرًا جزائيًا بنتيجة 0-2 لمخالفته اللوائح، مع منح نقاط الفوز الثلاث للمريخ، وهو ما ترتب عليه تغيير ترتيب المنافسة واعتلاء الفريق الأحمر صدارة الترتيب، ليصبح اللقب من نصيبه. ولم يتقبل الهلال القرار، مؤكدًا قانونية تسجيل لاعبيه، باعتبار أن عددًا منهم نالوا الجنسية السودانية، وتقدم بطلب مراجعة إلى لجنة الاستئنافات بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، التي قررت، الثلاثاء، إلغاء العقوبة الإدارية واعتماد نتيجة المباراة وفق تقرير الحكم، ليعود اللقب إلى الفريق الأزرق، بعد استعادة النقاط التي خسرها بقرار الرابطة. واحتفى الهلال بقرار اللجنة، معتبرًا أنه أعاد الحق للنادي، فيما وصف علي حسن عيسى، الأمين العام للنادي، القرار بأنه انتصار مهم لمجلس الإدارة، مشيرًا إلى نجاحه في حسم عدد من الملفات الإدارية والقانونية. الهلال السوداني لقب الدوري السوداني اترك تعليقاً إلغاء الرد لن يتم نشر عنوان بريدك الإلكتروني. football.content: المنتخب السوداني يصل داكار لمواجهة السنغال في تصفيات أمم أفريقيا - سودافاكس X الرئيسية الاخبار إقتصاد و أعمال منوعات عالمي مقالات الفيديو الصحة رياضة علوم وتكنولوجيا راسلنا سودافاكس المنتخب السوداني يصل داكار لمواجهة السنغال في تصفيات أمم أفريقيا تحرير سودافاكس 2026-11-11 أفادت مصادر بوصول بعثة المنتخب الوطني الأول لكرة القدم «صقور الجديان» إلى العاصمة السنغالية داكار مساء الثلاثاء. وتستعد البعثة لمواجهة «أسود التيرانغا» يوم الخميس 12 نوفمبر، ضمن الجولة الثالثة من التصفيات الأفريقية المؤهلة لنهائيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية. مدرب صقور الجديان : نلعب من أجل إسعاد الشعب السوداني يرأس البعثة نائب رئيس الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، المهندس أبو القاسم العوض، وتضم 26 لاعباً والجهازين الفني والإداري بقيادة المدرب الغاني كواسي أبياه. ومن الجانب الإداري عضو لجنة المنتخبات الوطنية محمد إبراهيم ميمي، ومدير المنتخب محمد نور صلاح الدين، ومساعده هيثم محمد نور. واستقبل البعثة في مطار داكار أسرة السفارة السودانية وأعضاء من الجالية السودانية والرابطة الرياضية، وأسهموا في إكمال إجراءات الدخول ومغادرة المطار في وقت وجيز. وقال السفير عبد الغني النعيم عوض الكريم إن السفارة والجالية حريصتان على تقديم كل أشكال الدعم للمنتخب، متمنياً أن يترجم اللاعبون وأعضاء الجهازين تحضيراتهم إلى نتائج تحقق تطلعات الشعب السوداني وتعزز حظوظ الفريق في مواصلة مشواره نحو النهائيات. من جانبه، أشاد العوض بحفاوة الاستقبال، وخص السفير بالشكر على حضوره الشخصي، معتبراً أن ذلك دافع معنوي للاعبين والجهازين قبل المباراة. وقرر الجهاز الفني منح اللاعبين راحة بعد الوصول، عقب رحلة طويلة من العاصمة الرواندية كيجالي عبر مدينة كانو إلى داكار. ويؤدي الفريق مرانه الرئيسي مساء الأربعاء. مقالات ذات صلة مواجهة من العيار الثقيل .. صقور الجديان يرفعون التحدي أمام السنغال مقترح مثير لاستكمال تأهيل المدينة الرياضية تعرف علي منافسي الهلال السوداني في دور مجموعات أبطال أفريقيا صحفي سوداني يشن هجوماً عنيفاً على إدارة نادي المريخ Leave a Comment 2026 جميع الحقوق محفوظة سودافاكس Exit mobile version
